attempts.plan:
1. Load the table of 33 boroughs into a pandas DataFrame.  
2. Compute the CHANGE column = first_half_2020_value − second_half_2019_value for every borough.  
3. Handle missing values: drop any borough that has a NaN in either original period; they cannot contribute to the change or to spatial statistics. (At most two rows removed, leaving ≥31 boroughs.)  
4. Build a binary spatial‐weights matrix W from the neighbor list:  
   • W_ij = 1 if borough i is listed as a neighbor of borough j, else 0 (and W_ii = 0).  
   • Row-standardize so each row sums to 1, giving weights w_ij = W_ij / Σ_j W_ij.  
5. Compute Global Moran’s I for the CHANGE vector x:  
   • x̄ = mean(x).  
   • Numerator = n Σ_i Σ_j w_ij (x_i − x̄)(x_j − x̄).  
   • Denominator = Σ_i (x_i − x̄)².  
   • I = Numerator / Denominator.  
6. Assess significance with a permutation test (Monte-Carlo randomization):  
   • Randomly permute the CHANGE values among boroughs 999 times (≥500 required).  
   • For each permutation, recalculate Moran’s I to build the null distribution.  
   • Two-sided p-value = (count of |I_rand| ≥ |I_obs| + 1) / (999 + 1).  
7. Interpret:  
   • If p < 0.05 and I > 0, conclude CHANGE is spatially clustered (similar changes cluster together).  
   • If p < 0.05 and I < 0, conclude negative spatial autocorrelation (neighbors tend to have opposite changes).  
   • If p ≥ 0.05, conclude the CHANGE shows no spatial clustering.  
8. Report the observed Moran’s I and permutation p-value, and state whether borough changes are CLUSTERED or NOT CLUSTERED.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# 1. Load the data -------------------------------------------------------------
crime_path = "chunks_csv/changespillover/changespillover_no2crime_crime_second_half_2019_to_first_half_2020.csv"
adj_path   = "chunks_csv/borough_adjacency.csv"

crime_df = pd.read_csv(crime_path)
adj_df   = pd.read_csv(adj_path)

# 2. Compute change and drop missing rows -------------------------------------
crime_df["change"] = crime_df["first_half_2020_value"] - crime_df["second_half_2019_value"]
crime_df = crime_df.dropna(subset=["change"]).reset_index(drop=True)   # at most two boroughs removed
n = len(crime_df)

# 3. Build a symmetric, row-standardised spatial-weights matrix ---------------
# Map borough name -> index in the retained DataFrame
idx = {b: i for i, b in enumerate(crime_df["borough"])}

# Start with a 0/1 adjacency matrix
W = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=float)
for _, row in adj_df.iterrows():
    b1, b2 = row["borough"], row["neighbor"]
    # only keep links where BOTH boroughs survived the drop-na step
    if b1 in idx and b2 in idx:
        i, j = idx[b1], idx[b2]
        W[i, j] = 1
        W[j, i] = 1          # make symmetric

# Row-standardise (so every row sums to 1) – rows with no neighbours remain 0
row_sums = W.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    W = np.where(row_sums > 0, W / row_sums, 0)

# 4. Compute Global Moran’s I --------------------------------------------------
x = crime_df["change"].to_numpy()
x_bar = x.mean()
v = x - x_bar

numerator   = n * v @ W @ v
denominator = (v ** 2).sum()
I_obs = numerator / denominator

# 5. Permutation test (999 random shuffles) -----------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_perm = 999
I_null = np.empty(n_perm)

for k in range(n_perm):
    x_perm = rng.permutation(x)
    v_perm = x_perm - x_perm.mean()
    I_null[k] = n * v_perm @ W @ v_perm / denominator

# two-sided p-value
p_val = (np.sum(np.abs(I_null) >= abs(I_obs)) + 1) / (n_perm + 1)

# 6. Verdict -------------------------------------------------------------------
verdict = "CLUSTERED" if (p_val < 0.05 and I_obs > 0) else "NOT CLUSTERED"

# 7. Required prints -----------------------------------------------------------
print(f"data_points_used = {n}")
print(f"FINAL ANSWER: {verdict} (Moran_I = {I_obs}, p = {p_val})")
